notes.meaning: The Lord gives Moses rules for any man or woman who freely chooses to take a Nazirite vow. The name Nazirite means someone who is separated or set apart. This vow allowed everyday Israelites, not just priests, to dedicate themselves completely to God for a specific period of time.

A Nazirite had to abstain from wine, fermented drinks, and every product of the grapevine, including fresh grapes, raisins, seeds, and skins. Staying away from all of these kept a person sober and watchful against temptation. It served as a physical reminder to put aside bodily pleasures to focus entirely on the Lord.

No razor was allowed to touch the person's head for the entire duration of the vow. Letting the hair grow long served as an obvious outward sign that the person belonged to God. It showed a willingness to set aside personal appearance and grooming to honor the Lord with their full strength and life.

A Nazirite was forbidden to go near any dead body, even if their own father, mother, brother, or sister died. In the law, death was closely linked to the curse of sin, so avoiding dead bodies preserved high ceremonial purity. Like the high priest, the Nazirite was called to put their devotion to God above even the closest family loyalties.

Throughout the whole period of the vow, the Nazirite remained holy to the Lord. The outward rules about food, hair, and purity were meaningful because they pointed to a heart genuinely dedicated to God's service.

If someone dropped dead unexpectedly next to a Nazirite, that sudden contact made the consecrated hair ceremonially unclean. The Nazirite had to undergo a seven-day cleansing process and shave off the defiled hair on the seventh day. Because the hair had touched defilement, it could no longer serve as a holy sign.

On the eighth day, the person brought two turtledoves or two young pigeons to the priest at the tabernacle. The priest offered one bird as a sin offering and the other as a burnt offering to make atonement, which means making things right with God through sacrifice. Even though the defilement happened by accident, a sacrifice was required before the person could start fresh.

The Nazirite had to rededicate their entire vow to the Lord and offer a young male lamb as a guilt offering. None of the days completed before the defilement were counted toward the vow, so the whole time period had to start over from day one. This strict rule showed the seriousness of keeping one's word before God.

When the full time of the vow was completed, the Nazirite was brought to the entrance of the tabernacle. Releasing the person from the vow took place in public so the whole community would know the commitment had been properly fulfilled.

The Nazirite presented several flawless animal sacrifices: a male lamb for a burnt offering of complete devotion, a female lamb for a sin offering, and a ram for a peace offering. These were accompanied by grain offerings, drink offerings, and a basket of unleavened bread and wafers. These costly gifts acknowledged that even after their best efforts, the worshiper still needed God's forgiveness and grace.

The priest presented these offerings to the Lord, sacrificing the sin offering first to clean away guilt and then the burnt offering. After that, he sacrificed the ram as a peace offering alongside the unleavened bread, grain, and drink offerings. The peace offering provided a fellowship meal that celebrated restored harmony and joy with God.

At the entrance of the tabernacle, the Nazirite shaved off their long hair and placed it into the altar fire beneath the peace offering. Since human beings could not be offered on the altar, burning the hair was a symbolic way of presenting their own strength and person to God. This solemn act brought the special separation to a close.

The priest took the boiled shoulder of the ram along with a cake and wafer from the basket, placed them into the Nazirite's hands, and waved them before the Lord. These portions became the priest's holy share, in addition to the standard breast and thigh from the peace offering. After this ceremony was complete, the Nazirite was entirely released from the vow and free to drink wine again.

These instructions gave the baseline requirement for anyone who made a Nazirite vow, though a person could also promise additional voluntary gifts if they were able. Whatever vow someone freely took upon themselves had to be fully and faithfully carried out.

The Lord commanded Moses to give Aaron and his sons the exact words they were to use when blessing the people of Israel. The priests were not left to invent their own blessing, because the power of the words came directly from God Himself. As official mediators, the priests spoke God's favor over the entire congregation.

The blessing opens by asking the Lord to pour out all good things on His people and to keep them safe. God's keeping power guards believers from evil, preserves them in faith, and protects them in daily life.

Asking the Lord to make His face shine means asking for His warm smile, favor, and delight, much like the sun bringing light and warmth to the earth. It also asks God to be gracious, showing that His undeserved kindness and mercy are the true source of all joy.

The third line asks the Lord to lift up His countenance toward His people, which means giving them His personal, loving attention and care. The peace requested here is not merely quietness, but complete wholeness, health, and well-being from God. Christian readers have long seen in this three-part repetition of the Lord's name a shadow of the Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

By speaking these words, the priests placed God's own name on the people of Israel, marking them as His chosen family and special possession. God attached a sure promise to this command, pledging that He Himself would personally bless them when this was done.
